C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from a ten-language monolingual/bilingual/multilingual family and broad open-ended-generation superiority claims to five principal monolingual models and their benchmark performance-cost tradeoff. v3 adds explicit open-release and sub-$1,000 training claims, and argues that language-specific modeling is the optimal strategy under resource constraints. Multilingual models remain supporting transfer experiments.

C2.justification: v3 adds morphological explanations for tokenization, interpolation-noise explanations for context-scaling behavior, and asymmetric transfer interpretations after instruction tuning. Its limitations newly connect weak broad-knowledge performance to restricted domains and discuss repeated-data overfitting and incomplete convergence. v2's limitations primarily concern translation quality and unfiltered outputs.

D1.justification: v3 supplies corpus provenance and sizes, architecture configurations, optimizer and learning-rate settings, batch sizes, gradient accumulation and training steps. Appendix B adds annotator qualifications, review procedures and translation post-editing details. It also documents a model/tokenizer/dataset collection link and CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 licensing, substantially extending v2's reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Tokenizer-fertility evaluation shifts from Assamese, Bangla, Hindi and Odia in v2 Figure 2 to Bangla, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and Telugu in v3 Figure 1. Dedicated Assamese/Odia cultural-prompt demonstrations disappear. The principal benchmark suite and broader multilingual coverage remain, despite the main narrative narrowing to five languages.

E2.justification: v3 Tables 9–13 substantially expand the evaluated comparators, adding BanglaT5, BanglaByT5, xGLM variants, mGPT, Llama-3/3.2, Aya23, Indic-Gemma-Navrasa and Nemotron-Hindi where applicable. Human comparisons also change: Figure 4 adds newer multilingual models while dropping the earlier quantitative comparisons with GPT2-XL, GPT-Neo, GPT-J, OPT and Llama-2.

E3.justification: v3 introduces tokenizer/cleaning controls, varying-context experiments and model-size/training-duration comparisons. Human evaluation changes from four to ten prompts, specifies ten annotators, and evaluates Hindi 367M rather than the earlier 162M model. Benchmark captions change ARC from normalized accuracy to accuracy; this is a reported metric revision, without establishing that retained scores were recomputed.

E4.justification: v3 Tables 4–5 add systematic ablations of Unigram vocabulary augmentation, data cleaning and positional-interpolation/context settings across five languages. Model-size and training-duration comparisons also expand. The earlier n-shot analysis is retained, while the Konkani-Maithili tokenizer comparison and much of the extensive generation-case-study material are removed.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports Fleiss kappa for instruction annotation (0.87) and human evaluation (0.85 Bengali, 0.79 Hindi, 0.72 Sanskrit), plus mean-plus/minus token-length statistics in Table 8. Benchmark seed variability and confidence intervals remain unreported. Colored training traces explicitly represent resumed runs, not independent repeated trials.

E6.justification: Numerous comparator, ablation and MFU results are added. Reported entries also change: Bangla MMLU is 23.82 in v2 Table 5 versus 24.82 in v3 Table 9; Hindi-instruct's Marathi average changes from 29.52 to 25.54. v3 retains Hindi's 29.92 fixed-duration result and adds 30.97 after extended training. Detailed generation outputs and Sanskrit rating tables are removed; the revised human study is not directly comparable.

M1.justification: The underlying approach remains from-scratch causal language modeling with BPE/Unigram tokenization, RoPE shrinking and instruction tuning. v3 explains vocabulary fusion, positional interpolation and architectural choices much more fully, but these disclosures do not establish a change to the underlying procedure. Additional model sizes are experimental configurations.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten, and the seventeen-item contribution list becomes four focused contributions. Background/decoding tutorials and lengthy model-demonstration narratives are removed. Methodology, experiments and discussion become distinct sections, and the single appendix is reorganized into topic-specific Appendices A–E.

P2.justification: v3 adds a consolidated benchmark summary, ablation tables, a RoPE diagram, a human-rating chart and training plots. Detailed benchmark tables move to the appendix; perplexity and CPU results are combined with MFU. Most generation screenshots and comparison tables disappear, while selected tokenizer and GPT-3.5 examples are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around language adaptation, morphology-aware tokenization and small monolingual models, including BanglaT5, BanglaByT5 and LLäMmlein. It newly credits Chen et al.'s positional interpolation and Bostrom and Durrett's tokenization findings. This replaces much of v2's adapter-centered discussion with a broader argument for training Indian-only models from scratch.

T1.justification: The explicit normalized human-rating definition accompanying v2 Table 12 disappears with that analysis. v3's positional-interpolation equation and worked example make the previously described shrinking rule explicit rather than establishing a new theoretical result. Neither version supplies a theorem or proof for the approach.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's sparse reproducibility information and limited isolation of component effects through detailed training/data documentation and controlled tokenizer, cleaning and context experiments. Broader evaluated comparisons and more substantive limitations make the central claims easier to assess. Removing detailed qualitative outputs loses useful evidence, and inconsistencies remain, notably ARC metric labeling and the monotonic-context claim contradicted by Table 5. These shortcomings temper but do not outweigh the substantial gains in methodological transparency and empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the Paramanu research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are sufficiently readable to match retained material and identify substantive revisions despite extensive restructuring.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark evaluations, tokenizer and context-scaling ablations, human ratings, annotation-agreement statistics and training measurements in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, perplexities, CPU inference measurements, human ratings and generated-text examples, including extensive appendix results.

results.title: Paramanu: Compact and Competitive Monolingual Language Models for Low-Resource Morphologically Rich Indian Languages

C1.justification: The central SciEvents-plus-EXCEEDS contributions remain. V2 removes the assertion that SciEvents is the first scientific event-extraction dataset and replaces the introduction's superiority-on-all-tasks claim with consistently strong performance. Event correlation remains part of the work but is no longer a separately enumerated contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning abstract-only data, missing multimodal/full-text information and restricted ACL/NLP coverage. Its new error interpretation identifies missed nuggets and semantically similar labels as major bottlenecks, extending v1's discussion of complex-form rarity and the original model components.

D1.justification: V2 adds decoding pseudocode, grid/warm-up/dropout hyperparameters, GPU specifications, runtime information, TextEE and baseline-adaptation details, and much richer annotation guidance. It supplies a concrete repository address where v1 only mentions GitHub. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation, although v1's explicit AdamW optimizer specification is omitted.

E1.justification: Extraction training and evaluation remain on SciEvents' 2,508 ACL 2019–2022 abstracts, with the same event schema and discontinuous, overlapping, reverse-order and sub-event scenarios. V2 broadens descriptive comparisons with other corpora, but adds no extraction benchmark. The DICE/Maccrobat-EE statistical comparison is retained under a different name.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains OneIE, PAIE and BartGen, removes UIE, and adds ScentedEAE, EEQA, Tagprime, DEEIA, DEGREE and KnowCoder. The complex-scenario comparison also expands substantially, including BartGen, which appeared only in v1's main comparison.

E3.justification: EXCEEDS changes from BERT, batch size 1 and 30 epochs to RoBERTa-large, batch size 2 and 20 epochs. Tagprime replaces the word-word relation model supplying triggers to retained argument-only baselines. The split ratio and five core metrics remain, but Table 4 stops reporting trigger classification for discontinuous and reverse-order subsets.

E4.justification: Biaffine/BiAttention ablations are replaced by Contextual/Grid Refiner ablations, also evaluated on complex subsets. V2 adds identification-error and type-confusion analyses in Figures 4–5, computational-cost measurements, and detailed analyses of document length and complex-structure distributions in Appendix H.

E5.justification: V1 reports averages from at least three experiments without dispersion estimates. V2 specifies three independent runs and introduces systematic ± uncertainty reporting across overall, complex-scenario and ablation results. The meaning of ± is not defined, and neither an increase in runs nor significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: Result sets are extensively replaced and expanded. Table 3 reports EXCEEDS AC/EC F1 of 41.85/47.60 in v1 and 43.20/48.25 for the revised setup in v2; these are not controlled performance gains. OneIE now leads TI. V2 also adds numerous baseline, error-analysis, runtime and dataset-statistics results.

M1.justification: Sections 5.2–5.3 replace v1's CLN-generated grid and combined Biaffine/BiAttention predictions with token normalization, pair representations incorporating distance embeddings, and residual convolutional grid refinement. Cross-entropy/softmax prediction becomes multi-label categorical cross-entropy with zero-threshold decisions. These change the architecture, objective and inference procedure while retaining the HTL/THL/EAL concept.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and dataset narrative are extensively rewritten, with clearer organization around density and complexity. Annotation procedures, remuneration and distributions are reorganized into appendices, and schema explanations are expanded. The title, acronym expansion and complex-nugget terminology also change.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the motivating example and architecture, adds a grid illustration and error plots, and removes v1's dataset-construction diagram. The main results table becomes an F1 summary with ablation rows, while precision/recall results move to appendix tables. Distribution displays are redesigned and expanded, and annotation screenshots are added.

R1.justification: V2 develops a more specific comparison with approaches including RexUIE, Mirror and KnowCoder, positioning EXCEEDS around raw-text input and an EE-only, single-dataset setting. Citations are substantially revised for newer methods and resources, while v1's explicit connection to Li et al.'s word-word NER approach is removed.

T1.justification: Appendix D newly derives componentwise computational and memory scaling, including O(l²Cg + l²|R|) grid storage. Appendix A discusses potentially exponentially many candidate decoding paths. V1 contains neither analysis; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation and reproducibility through broader baseline comparisons, uncertainty reporting, diagnostic analyses, and detailed decoding, implementation and annotation documentation. Explicit applicability limits and narrower superiority claims improve calibration. Undefined ± statistics and a remaining mismatch between the claimed uniform grid-refiner benefit and Table 3's TI result limit these gains, but the overall improvement in evidence and assessability is substantial. Changed settings prevent treating higher scores as controlled architectural gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SciEvents and EXCEEDS, retaining the same underlying corpus and task schema despite substantial revisions. Text, equations, tables, figures and all appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original extraction experiments and ablations, supplemented by error analyses, runtime measurements and detailed dataset analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original SciEvents dataset statistics, extraction experiments, complex-scenario evaluations and model ablations in Tables 1–5.

results.title: EXCEEDS: Extracting Complex Events via Nugget-based Grid Modeling in Scientific Domain

C1.justification: The evaluation-framework contribution and central claim that collaboration affects coding outcomes remain. The conclusion now explicitly qualifies effects by system and corpus and highlights topic modeling's strongest correctness performance on Climate, refining v5's emphasis on topic-model shortcomings.

C2.justification: Section 5.3 replaces v5's correctness explanation centered on interaction-induced biases with a corpus-dependent account, suggesting that longer Climate documents and a smaller corpus help topic modeling. Recommendations now explicitly reject a universally best configuration. This materially changes the interpretation of system performance; the stated limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: V6 supplies a repository link and states that code and experimental data are available, replacing v5's future release promise. It additionally documents SBERT use, approximate integer-linear inference, and learned rule weights more explicitly, and revises compute accounting. These are disclosure and access-information changes, not demonstrated algorithm changes.

E1.justification: Both versions use 85,799 COVID vaccine tweets and 5,471 Climate ads for synchronous and asynchronous thematic coding, with the same reported participant population. The additional Climate correctness results concern an already evaluated corpus and task.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparison set remains Fang et al.'s topic-model system, Pacheco et al.'s relational system, and the Chew et al.-based LLM workflow. The added Climate correctness comparison uses these same three approaches; no comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Section 5.3 extends correctness evaluation to Climate, increasing the reported sample from 1,200 to 2,400 pairs while retaining quartile stratification, 200 pairs per setting, and adjudication. Section 4 revises the stated experiment total from 15 to 30, and the LLM appendix changes five jobs to ten. These reporting revisions do not establish reruns of retained experiments.

E4.justification: The correctness-versus-theme-distance analysis now includes Climate, adding evidence about reliability as progressively less-related documents are included. The existing top-quartile cohesiveness checks, corpus-characterization analyses, and interviews are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 1–2 now explicitly identify their parenthesized values as standard deviations; v5 leaves these values unspecified. The values, unpaired t-tests, and significance thresholds remain unchanged. Climate annotator agreement extends the existing reporting practice rather than introducing a new statistical procedure.

E6.justification: Figure 4 adds materially different Climate findings: at 'All', synchronous topic-model F1 is approximately 0.81 and synchronous relational F1 approximately 0.47. COVID curves and Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. V6 also adds Climate Krippendorff's alpha of 0.696, Climate prompt-agreement and unlabeled-document results in Table 4, and detailed theme outputs, counts, and overlaps in Tables 11–17 and Figures 9–11.

M1.justification: The QDTM, relational, and Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct coding workflows remain the same. Section 3.2 expands the explanation of relational inference and learned concept–theme rules; comparison with v5's Section 3 and Appendix C establishes additional documentation, rather than a new algorithm component.

P1.justification: V6 substantially expands system explanations, revises the results narrative and conclusion, and reorganizes the appendices. Relational settings move into Section 3.2, dataset analysis moves from Appendix A to C, LLM details from E to B, and interviews from D to F. These changes exceed simple renumbering.

P2.justification: Figure 4 becomes a two-panel correctness plot, Tables 11–17 add codebooks and counts, and Figures 9–11 add paired heatmaps. Existing prompt boxes become captioned Figures 5–8, Figures 2–3 are reformatted, and table captions and placement change. The prompt displays and relocated dataset tables are retained content.

R1.justification: The bibliography contains the same works, and the related-work discussion retains the same positioning around collaborative qualitative coding and standardized evaluation. Its edits change exposition without substantively changing relationships to prior research.

T1.justification: The evaluation definitions remain unchanged, and neither version supplies new theoretical results or proofs. V6's soft-rule example and integer-linear-inference description elaborate the retained relational system without introducing a distinct formal result or revised mathematical argument.

improvement.justification: V6 resolves v5's missing correctness evaluation for one of its two central corpora. The contrasting Climate results materially improve the basis for system comparisons and corpus-specific recommendations, rather than merely adding supporting scores. Detailed codebooks, alignment results, and reported code/data access also improve transparency. Explanations attributing performance to corpus length and size remain hypotheses, but the overall empirical and interpretive gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with the same title, authors, systems, and datasets. Text extraction and visual inspection, including all appendices, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V6 retains these original empirical results and additionally reports Climate correctness evaluation, prompt-agreement results, and detailed coding outputs.

before.justification: V5 reports original coding experiments, quantitative comparisons on two corpora, manual correctness evaluation on COVID tweets, corpus analyses, and participant interviews.

results.title: Effects of Collaboration on the Performance of Interactive Theme Discovery Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the core contributions: constructing preference data from in-situ feedback and evaluating alignment using user-derived preferences. The shorter abstract and renamed evaluation do not materially redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets checklist judging as performing approximately on par with humans and emphasizes superiority over UltraFeedback in its results discussion. The latter wording exceeds the mixed results in Table 3. The substantive limitations concerning harmful preferences and feedback selection bias remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds the UltraFeedback construction prompt in Appendix A.4, reports approximately 8 A100 GPU hours for SFT and 24 for DPO, and documents software licensing and WildChat's privacy processing and identifiers. These are additional disclosures; core training settings remain, and both versions still promise future dataset availability.

E1.justification: UltraFeedback moves from a descriptive dataset comparison in v1 to actual baseline training data in v2, adding curated instruction prompts. WildChat and the AlpacaEval 2, MT-Bench, Arena-Hard, and WildFeedback evaluation tasks remain.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated UF GPT-4 and UF On-policy training baselines for each model family in Table 3 and Figure 3; v1 compares WildFeedback-trained models with their off-the-shelf counterparts. Qwen 2 also replaces Mistral in the reported model comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces UltraFeedback construction protocols using two GPT-4 responses or five on-policy candidates per prompt, and a human validation study with 200 conversations, six annotators, and adjudication. Qwen2-7B replaces Mistral-7B. Existing benchmark metrics, 540-example test-set construction, and SFT/DPO hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix C directly examines the reliability of checklist-guided judging against human annotations, addressing an evaluation component not human-validated in v1. Figure 3 also extends the with/without-checklist analysis to UltraFeedback comparisons. The earlier SAT/DSAT validation remains.

E5.justification: Both versions report aggregate scores and agreement statistics without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Table 7 extends agreement reporting to a new validation study; it does not introduce run-to-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds UltraFeedback and human-validation results and replaces Mistral results with Qwen 2 results. Retained entries also change: Phi 3 WF On-policy AlpacaEval LC rises from 24.2 to 29.0 and Arena-Hard from 22.0 to 30.1. LLaMA 3 WF GPT-4's without-checklist win percentage changes from 48.1 in v1 Table 3 to 59.9 in v2 Figure 3. These are reported updates, not evidence that model replacement produced comparable gains.

M1.justification: The SAT/DSAT identification, preference extraction, response generation, on-policy filtering, and SFT followed by DPO remain unchanged. Appendix A.1–A.3 prompts are substantively retained. Renaming user-guided evaluation to checklist-guided evaluation and replacing an experimental backbone do not introduce a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, methods, and results are rewritten or condensed. Evaluation terminology changes throughout, the conclusion moves before limitations, SAT/DSAT annotation details move into Appendix B.2, and the appendix structure expands and is renumbered.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. Table 1 is reorganized, and WildFeedback results formerly within Table 3 become an expanded stacked-bar Figure 3. v2 adds Table 7 and Figure 5; the earlier annotation-interface figure is retained as Figure 4.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature supporting annotator disagreement and synthetic-feedback bias, plus references motivating UltraFeedback response regeneration. Its introduction more explicitly distinguishes earlier structured-feedback and direct fine-tuning approaches. The broad positioning relative to SPUR, WildBench, and existing preference datasets remains.

T1.justification: Neither version supplies theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The feedback rubrics and operational definitions are retained; the added agreement results do not introduce new theory.

improvement.justification: v1 lacks a trained alternative-data baseline, leaving WildFeedback's advantage over generic preference fine-tuning unresolved. v2's UltraFeedback controls and human agreement study substantially strengthen the evidence for its data and evaluation contributions. There are tradeoffs: Mistral's adverse on-policy results disappear, and claims of consistent UltraFeedback superiority overstate Table 3, where Qwen 2 WF GPT-4 has lower LC than UF GPT-4 (39.4 versus 40.6). Nevertheless, the new controls and direct assessment of judge reliability address important evidential gaps.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WildFeedback. All 24 pages of each version, including appendices, tables, figures, and prompts, support comparison despite extensive reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical experiments and adds UltraFeedback training comparisons and human validation of checklist-guided evaluation in Appendix C and Table 7.

before.justification: v1 reports original feedback classification, human annotation, preference-data analysis, and fine-tuning experiments, including Tables 3 and 6 and Figure 2.

results.title: WildFeedback: Aligning LLMs With In-situ User Interactions And Feedback

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion redefine TrendFact's central contribution around hotspot perception across retrieval, verification and explanation, extending the earlier emphasis on Chinese explanations. HCPI and the dated evidence library become central contributions, and FactISR becomes a three-component method. The broad claims that existing models struggle and FactISR helps remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations attributing higher HCPI to RLM reasoning about hotspot attributes and DEA efficiency to reduced noisy evidence and redundant reasoning. These extend the existing discussion without replacing its explanation of concise RLM outputs and lower lexical scores. The labor-cost limitations in Section 7 remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands documentation with staged filtering prompts, claim-rewriting factors, annotation-review criteria, evidence-library construction instructions, and HCPI weights, imputation and scaling. Hardware changes from four to two A100 GPUs. Some earlier specifics disappear, including GPT-3.5 implementation details for traditional baselines and the three-independent-reviewer count. The code/data access statement remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 7,643 Chinese claims from trending platforms and CHEF. v3 adds an evaluated retrieval task over a 66,217-entry evidence library with publication dates, plus verification and explanation under retrieved-evidence conditions. This substantially expands task coverage and the evidence conditions encountered during evaluation.

E2.justification: v3 adds QwQ-32B and Qwen3-32B thinking/non-thinking comparisons, alongside BM25 with/without dates, text-embedding-ada-002 and bge-m3 retrieval comparisons. PROGRAM-FC and CLAIMDECOMP remain. The explicit QwQ-Preview CoT comparator disappears, while o1-preview remains in the gold-evidence appendix rather than the new main comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 introduces retrieval R@1/2/3/5 and HCPI evaluation, retrieved-evidence experiments, and FactISR evaluations on two newer backbones. Appendix J changes the stated RLM output limit from v2's 300 to 5k, retaining 300 for LLMs, and specifies 3k retrieval truncation. Its three-addition DEA limit conflicts with the two-addition limit in Figure 9.

E4.justification: v2 incrementally adds ET and ISR on QwQ-Preview. v3 replaces this with separate removal of DEA, ET and ISR on two backbones (Table 5), adds DEA generation-time/input-evidence-length analysis (Table 6), and presents a new DEA case (Figure 10). The original cold-wave reflection example is retained as translated Figure 11.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or comparable uncertainty analyses. Both present point estimates; the additional results do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds retrieval, HCPI, retrieved-evidence and efficiency results. For example, bge-m3 achieves R@5 of 78.97, and FactISR improves retrieved-evidence QwQ-32B accuracy from 72.67 to 74.32. Every retained standalone gold-evidence baseline score matches v2 exactly in Tables 10–11; the earlier CoT/ET/ET+ISR rows are removed. The new main scores are not same-setting changes from v2.

M1.justification: v2 FactISR combines evidence triangulation and rewarded self-reflection. v3 adds Dynamic Evidence Augmentation, which inserts additional retrieved evidence during reasoning when the model emits an evidence-request signal (Section 4.2; Figures 9–10). This changes the inference procedure; the existing triangulation workflow and reward-decoding equation are substantially retained.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites the abstract, motivation, contributions, construction narrative and results discussion. The former Baselines section becomes a dedicated FactISR section, comparator descriptions move into experimental setup, and the appendices are extensively reorganized. The title, author order and contact information also change.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redesigned to include hotspot attributes, evidence-library construction and DEA. Table 1 gains hotspot and task columns, and new retrieval, ablation and efficiency tables restructure the results presentation. Earlier gold-evidence results and ECS definitions move to appendices; new workflow displays appear, and the reflection example is translated and reformatted.

R1.justification: v3 substantially repositions TrendFact against prior benchmarks around missing hotspot assessment and comprehensive task coverage (Section 2; Table 1), extending the earlier Chinese-explanation gap. It adds BGE-M3, DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3 references while removing several Wikipedia, table and dialogue verification references.

T1.justification: Appendix F adds formal influence and HCPI definitions (Equations 2–3), combining risk-weighted logarithmic hotspot indicators, ECS and asymmetric label-error penalties. This introduces a substantive new mathematical evaluation framework, although some predicted-label cases are unspecified. The reward-decoding equation and five-level ECS definition remain unchanged; no proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important evaluation gap by testing evidence retrieval and verification with retrieved evidence, while retaining the standalone gold-evidence results. Detailed construction workflows and two-backbone ablations substantially strengthen auditability and support for the method's components. These gains outweigh the loss of CoT/gold-evidence FactISR comparisons, although the inconsistent DEA limit and incomplete HCPI prediction cases remain material specification weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TrendFact and FactISR, retaining the same core dataset, method components and many results. The main text, equations, figures, tables and all appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and retitling.

after.justification: v3 Tables 2–6 report original retrieval, verification, explanation, ablation and efficiency results. Tables 10–11 also retain earlier gold-evidence results.

before.justification: v2 Tables 2–3 report original fact-verification, explanation-generation and component-evaluation results on TrendFact.

results.title: TrendFact: A Benchmark Towards Hotspot Perception in Automatic Fact-Checking

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes scalable lookup decoding, fourfold throughput at fixed short-context latency, and effectiveness across tasks. v2 makes deployment without data preparation, cold-start operation, automatic language/domain adaptation, and robustness under distribution shift central contributions. Its abstract and conclusion also foreground competitiveness with trained approaches. This substantially changes the contribution emphasis and scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking adaptation to model-generated datastore contents and long-context advantages to approximately constant drafting cost without a draft KV-cache. It explains cases where EAGLE-3 performs better. The new Limitations section qualifies v1’s optimistic MoE discussion and adds MLA-kernel, CPU, and host-memory constraints; Appendix B explicitly excludes communication costs. Privacy and cross-language performance implications are also newly discussed.

D1.justification: Appendix A expands the single merging pseudocode into retrieval and merging algorithms with explicit thresholds and dampening constants. v2 adds datastore, generation, and deployment details, including a 13 GB datastore, and promises code release upon acceptance without establishing public availability. Some v1 details, including OpenMP and CPU identification, disappear. Appendix C’s TP = 2 description conflicts with Figure 6’s one-GPU-per-stage caption.

E1.justification: v2 retains MT-Bench, GSM8k, and PG-19, but removes the Natural Questions short-query and Dolly-15k evaluations. It adds HumanEval code generation, SWE-Bench agentic workloads, MATH-500 including extended reasoning, and multilingual MT-Bench translations. Cold-start and language-adaptation scenarios substantially broaden the evaluated conditions.

E2.justification: v1 compares candidate quality against REST and PIA, and end-to-end performance against autoregressive decoding and PIA. v2 adds evaluated PLD, EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3, and Llama-3.2-1B draft-model baselines; REST also enters end-to-end comparisons. PIA and v2’s Lookahead refer to the same Zhao et al. method and are matched as a retained comparator.

E3.justification: The customized vLLM/Ascend setup is replaced by SGLang/GPU experiments using newer 8B models, Qwen3-14B, and Llama-3.3-70B. New protocols include prefill/decode disaggregation, tensor parallelism, and stochastic reasoning generation up to 4096 tokens. Single-device totals still include prefill, whereas distributed plots report inter-token latency. These changes prevent treating the results as same-setting reruns.

E4.justification: The candidate-source ablation is retained and revised, while v2 adds datastore-size sensitivity, empty versus English-initialized datastores, language adaptation, and model-generated versus dataset-answer comparisons (Figure 4). Lookahead receives warm/cold-cache analysis. v1’s tokenizer comparison, temperature sweep, and empirical operator-cost breakdown are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: v2 first specifies averages over five runs for the Qwen3-14B experiments in Figure 4 and the reasoning experiment in Figure 5f. v1 supplies no corresponding repeated-run counts. Neither version reports confidence intervals or significance tests. This is additional run reporting, not evidence that previously reported experiments received more runs.

E6.justification: Much of the empirical evidence is replaced or expanded. For example, v1 Figure 6 reports 2.05x PG-19 speedup for Llama2-7b at batch size 1 and approximately 3400-token inputs. v2 Table 1 reports SSSD speedups of 1.23x/1.26x versus EAGLE-3’s 0.80x/1.09x for Llama-3.1-8B/Llama-3.3-70B with disaggregation and inputs up to 40k tokens. v2 also adds a 2.29x reasoning speedup. Different conditions preclude direct performance-change conclusions.

M1.justification: v2 extends v1’s fixed external datastore with online accumulation of outputs from past conversations and oldest-entry eviction, enabling empty-store startup and adaptation during serving (Section 3.1.2). This changes the method’s operation beyond the per-request prompt/self-output trie already present in v1. The underlying CPU retrieval and candidate-tree fusion approach remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around deployment and adaptation. Objectives become an explicit contributions list, evaluation sections are reorganized, and algorithm/hardware material moves into expanded appendices. Dedicated Limitations and Ethical considerations sections further change the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1 with datastore-update machinery, combines revised hardware/speedup plots into Figure 2, and introduces cold-start and multilingual panels. Earlier latency–cost plots and throughput bars give way to multi-baseline latency–throughput grids. The hardware table moves to Appendix B with revised rows, and a PG-19 results table is added. Typography, headers, and abstract layout also change.

R1.justification: v2 substantially develops positioning around multilingual disparities, domain adaptation, EAGLE-3, and multi-token prediction, including a new Multilinguality subsection and references to Yi et al., Sandler et al., and Hong et al. The earlier hybrid-method discussion, including TriForce and Ouroboros, is removed. Publication updates to retained works such as REST and MagicDec are not treated as new research.

T1.justification: v1 Table 1 assumes equal query and KV head counts. v2 Appendix B and Table 2 introduce explicit GQA group size and tensor-parallel size into the FLOP/IO derivations, revise MLP accounting, and change approximate attention intensity from 2sq to 2gsq. The resulting attention-versus-linear-layer bounds extend the mathematical model substantially beyond relocating the existing roofline discussion.

results.title: Analytical FFN-to-MoE Restructuring via Activation Pattern Analysis

results.title: Challenging the Boundaries of Reasoning: An Olympiad-Level Math Benchmark for Large Language Models

This substantially expands the claimed contribution and introduces process-level verification as a central feature.

It frames formal verification as a response to heuristic shortcuts and newly qualifies contamination protection as temporary after public release. The inability to quantify natural-language guessing remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: v3 supplies the formalization agent's full prompt, Mathlib v4.24.0, the Lean server interaction procedure, validation stages, and formal-prover generation settings and prompt sources (Section 4.2 and Appendix A.2). E1.justification: v3 adds the disjoint 150-problem OlymMATH-LEAN theorem-proving task, extending the benchmark from 200 to 350 unique problems. The original 100 EASY and 100 HARD bilingual numerical problems remain. PolyMath is additionally used in the new empirical leakage comparison.

E3.justification: The original numerical evaluation settings remain unchanged. v3 adds Pass@k evaluation for retained DeepSeek distillation models and a formal evaluation requiring successful Lean proofs, using 32 attempts per problem. The new leakage protocol compares five-gram continuation accuracy at five sampled positions against three rewritten versions (Sections 3.1 and 4).

E4.justification: v3 adds quantitative leakage analysis, sampling-budget and consensus comparisons, analysis of Chinese answer-extraction failures, and a detailed Lean error breakdown (Tables 2, 5 and 8). These address contamination, reliability and failure mechanisms beyond v2's analyses. The four earlier guessing case studies are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports Wilcoxon signed-rank testing of EN–ZH differences across 14 models and adds a binomial standard-error comparison between benchmark sizes. It also specifies 32 proof attempts for the new evaluation; the original 64/8-response sampling remains unchanged. Numerical test statistics, p-values and confidence intervals are not supplied.

E6.justification: All numerical score entries in v2 Tables 4–5 match v3 Tables 9–10. Substantial new results include leakage scores, Pass@k analyses and Lean performance/error rates: Lean Pass@32 is 14.00%, 8.67% and 10.00% for Kimina, DeepSeek V2 and Goedel V2, respectively. Cross-benchmark reporting adds OlympiadBench and Omni-MATH scores while removing the HMMT scores shown in v2 Figure 1.

M1.justification: v3 adds a substantive formalization and verification pipeline: an agent generates Lean statements and proofs, iteratively repairs them using compiler feedback, and undergoes semantic validation and conditional expert review (Section 3.1 and Appendix A.2). The existing numerical-answer construction and translation procedures are retained.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion around the expanded contribution, introduces dedicated Related Work and Limitations sections, and reorganizes experiments into natural-language and formal-language evaluations. Usability moves to the appendix, which gains named subsections. The author list and technical-report header also change.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, replaces the main full score tables with a bilingual representative-model table, and relocates complete results to the appendix. It adds several analytical tables, redraws the language and AIME comparison plots, revises the example figure, and removes v2's cross-benchmark bar chart and appendix boxplot.

R1.justification: A new Related Work section substantially broadens positioning to formal benchmarks including miniF2F, ProofNet, FIMO and PutnamBench, alongside PolyMath and AMO Bench. Additional literature contextualizes contamination, multilingual reasoning and heuristic shortcuts. The paper now positions its novelty around integrating numerical and formal evaluation.

T1.justification: v3 Figure 1 adds an explicit Lean theorem statement: a prime p dividing 2^n + 1 cannot satisfy p mod 8 = 7. This is a limited addition of formal mathematical content, presented with a proof placeholder. The retained appendix derivations are unchanged, and no new general theoretical analysis is supplied.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v2's sourcing-based contamination assurance and qualitative examples: Tables 2, 5 and 7–8 add leakage evidence, sampling reliability analysis and proof-evaluation error analysis, while Appendix A.2 makes formalization inspectable. These improve evidential support and reproducibility while preserving the original results. Important limits remain: Wilcoxon outputs are missing, the formalizer permits expert-reviewed axioms, and the separate Lean tasks do not quantify guessing in the numerical tasks.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OlymMATH, with clearly matchable methods, experiments and examples. All 15 pages of v2 and 20 pages of v3, including appendices, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those original evaluations and adds leakage analysis, sampling analyses and evaluations of three theorem-proving models on OlymMATH-LEAN.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of 28 models on English and Chinese OlymMATH problems, including category-level results in Tables 4–5 and model-output case studies.

results.title: Challenging the Boundaries of Reasoning: An Olympiad-Level Math Benchmark for Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central defense, efficiency and response-quality claims remain. v2 softens the loss's theoretical framing from being induced from a DPO upper bound to sharing its insights, and its discussion explicitly adds robustness and generalizability across attack types.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations concerning known context boundaries, trigger tokens as implicit planning, free-form QA metrics, and adaptive-attack optimization limitations. It also introduces an erroneous interpretation: Section 4.2 says increasing α raises ASR, reversing v1's explanation despite the retained table showing ASR falling from 13.50 to 6.40 as α increases from 0.3 to 1.5.

D1.justification: v2 supplies evaluation code snippets for F1, ROUGE and BERTScore, identifies gpt-4-1106-preview as the judge, and includes complete judging prompts. It also documents attack construction, initialization and optimization settings. Details about the retained free-form QA evaluation and sampling procedure are expanded without establishing changes to those original procedures.

E1.justification: SQuAD, HotpotQA and WildChat remain the datasets. v2 substantially expands adversarial test scenarios through controlled transfer across attack-instruction families and defense-adaptive GCG attacks, including transferred attack sequences (Figure 5 and Appendices F–G).

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Sandwich as an evaluated defense alongside the retained Vanilla, Delimiting, Datamarking and Encode_Base64 comparators. Newly discussed detection and attribution methods are cited rather than evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds Phi-3.5-mini-instruct (3.8B), attribution sample-size sweeps of 4/8/12, and ROUGE-1/2/L and BERTScore evaluation. Its new adaptive protocol optimizes attack tokens over 24 examples, normally using 10 tokens and 20 epochs, with 30-token and 100-epoch variants. Original default benchmark settings remain.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether restricting pruning to Φ preserves quality, sensitivity to attribution sample count, transfer across attack instructions, and robustness to adaptive attacks and their optimization budgets (Tables 5–12; Figures 5 and 9). The original token-count, masking-strength, pruning-ratio, layer-distribution and code/text transfer analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over three trials and use ± entries. v2 does not establish additional repetitions, seed disclosure or a new uncertainty-estimation practice. Added result rows and changed uncertainty values are changes to results.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial model, baseline, ablation, transfer, adaptive-attack and metric results. Table 7 reports adaptive-attack ASR of 7.71±0.63 for CachePrune versus 97.89 for Vanilla. Original benchmark means are retained, while Table 1's Llama3/SQuAD attack-F1 changes from 22.84±0.18 to 22.84±0.49. Some new deltas are inconsistent: Delimiting ASR rising from 23.60 to 100 implies +76.40, whereas Table 7 prints +72.14.

M1.justification: The probability-difference loss, activation-times-gradient attribution, maximum aggregation, normalized Φ restriction and context-cache masking are retained. The newly named attribution and intervention stages elaborate existing components. The threshold formula revision does not establish a change to the described top-fraction pruning procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Section 2 gains separate attribution and intervention subsections, while DPO motivation moves into Appendix B and baseline/metric descriptions move into Appendix A. Expanded appendices reorganize sampling explanations, evaluation details and analyses.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn, and v2 adds transfer heatmaps and adaptive-training plots. Table 1 gains model and baseline rows plus metric-direction indicators. Original ablation tables and layer histograms move into the appendices, alongside substantial new ablation, adaptive-attack and metric tables.

R1.justification: Section 3 substantially expands positioning relative to detection/filtering defenses and attribution/activation patching. It explicitly locates the contribution in using attribution to understand data versus instructions rather than introducing an entirely new intervention technique, and discusses shared context-boundary assumptions. Additional references support the new attacks, model and metrics.

T1.justification: Equation 5 revises the pruning-threshold formula from a supremum expression to an infimum expression using an indicator expectation. The DPO bound, entropy decomposition, Lemma 1 and their proofs are otherwise retained and relocated to Appendices B–D. The newly stated standard F1 formulas add explanation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the central robustness and quality-preservation claims through adaptive attacks, cross-attack transfer, the Φ ablation and additional quality metrics. Evaluation code and judging prompts address important reproducibility gaps in v1. These gains outweigh localized reporting errors, including the reversed α interpretation and incorrect Table 7 baseline deltas, although those errors weaken confidence in some explanations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CachePrune. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original model evaluations, ablations, cross-attack transfer tests, adaptive attacks and additional quality metrics.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on SQuAD, HotpotQA and WildChat, alongside pruning ablations, neuron analyses and code/text attack transfer results.

results.title: CachePrune: Teaching LLMs What Not to Follow via KV-Cache Editing

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion redefine the contribution from a competitive-programming benchmark into a complementary Comp/Repo suite assessing algorithmic reasoning and software-library functionality. Claims about multi-turn degradation and dependency difficulty remain, but the claimed empirical applicability now explicitly includes repository-derived software contexts.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations distinguishing shallow reasoning from capacity demands at greater dependency depth, and algorithmic errors from repository integration errors. It replaces the competition-only limitation with source-specific ingestion limitations and discussion of specialized models and debugging loops. Figure 12 also newly explains the non-monotonic relationship between structural complexity and difficulty at the simplest structures.

D1.justification: v3 adds evaluation templates and conditional prompt rules, repository import handling and Docker execution details, sampling tables, and pipeline token/cost estimates. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without proving changes to retained experiments. The forthcoming-release promise in v1 is replaced by explicit dataset and changed code-repository links.

E1.justification: The original 5,258 Codeforces problems are retained as CodeFlowBench-Comp. v3 adds evaluated repository-derived function-generation tasks covering Basic, Cryptography, Network, System, and Visualization domains. This substantially extends coverage beyond competitive programming; DomainEval's Computation domain is explicitly excluded.

E2.justification: Table 1 changes from 13 to 19 models, adding GPT-5 variants, o3-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini-2.5/3, Claude-4/4.5, and Qwen3 models. GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Yi-Coder, and QwQ leave this main comparison. GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet remain in the DSC comparison in v3 Figure 16.

E3.justification: v1 specifies the most recent 20% of problems for testing. v3 specifies 1,000 problems, but Section 4 calls them the most recent whereas Appendix E.1 describes depth-stratified sampling. This is a reported protocol revision without establishing reruns. v3 also introduces APT evaluation and new semantic, stylistic, and five-criterion quality-assessment protocols.

E4.justification: Appendix A.6 adds cross-model description-consistency tests, solution-decomposition sensitivity checks, and human/LLM subproblem-quality validation. Error analysis expands to repository tasks and Gemini-3-Flash. Conversely, v1's IR-remediation study is removed. The original four error-case illustrations are retained in v3 Appendix F.2.

E5.justification: v3 adds a sampling-distribution chi-square test with p=0.1246 and alpha=0.05, plus a variance-motivated PD@k estimation procedure in Appendix D. Neither version specifies actual repeated-run counts, seeds, or confidence intervals for the benchmark scores; the new estimator does not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive model, repository, APT, and validation results. Table 1 newly reports Gemini-3-flash-thinking at 48.4%/65.5% multi-turn/single-turn Pass@1 on Comp and GPT-5 at 34.7%/48.8% on Repo. Retained Comp entries such as o1-mini's 20.8%/37.8% are unchanged. v1's IR-remediation results of 16.7% and 8.3% disappear. These additions do not establish same-setting performance improvements between versions.

M1.justification: The core AST-based decomposition, dependency ordering, test capture, and iterative generation procedure remain. Appendix C.2 introduces a limited repository-specific adaptation: DomainEval reference functions and tests are used directly, omitting the solution-verification step before dependency analysis.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and results discussion are extensively rewritten. The six-stage pipeline presentation is condensed into two phases, discussion is integrated into the experiments section, and the appendices are reorganized into A–G with a contents list. Existing pipeline details and error cases remain identifiable across these moves.

P2.justification: v3 changes to a two-column layout, redraws the introductory diagrams, expands the main table into Comp/Repo panels, and adds APT, validation, and sampling tables. The turn-performance plots change from four panels to two. Dataset statistics and the expanded DSC heatmap move to the appendices, while original screenshot examples are retained.

R1.justification: v3 expands positioning through DomainEval, agile-development and code-reuse literature, and additional software-engineering benchmarks. Appendix C.1 explicitly distinguishes constructive function generation from repository maintenance tasks. Earlier discussion and citations concerning TreeInstruct, EvoCodeBench, and DS-1000 are removed, substantially revising the research context.

T1.justification: v1 defines PD(k) as the maximum observed depth over k attempts. v3 Appendix D defines an expected maximum and derives an unbiased estimator using ordered depths from n trials and combinatorial weights. This adds substantive mathematical definition and reasoning beyond the original metric description.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's competition-only limitation through evaluations on repository-derived functions across five domains, strengthening the empirical basis for its real-world-workflow claims. Pipeline validation and detailed evaluation templates also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of the IR-remediation analysis. However, conflicting sampling descriptions and an explicitly permissive quality-scoring prompt remain material weaknesses and limit confidence in some stronger interpretations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CodeFlowBench. The original benchmark is identifiable as CodeFlowBench-Comp in v3, and the complete text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds repository-derived tasks, additional model results, pipeline ablations, and human/LLM quality assessments.

before.justification: v1 reports original multi-turn and single-turn model evaluations, dependency-complexity analyses, error distributions, and an IR-remediation study.

results.title: CodeFlowBench: A Multi-turn, Iterative Benchmark for Complex Code Generation

C1.justification: The automatic synthesis and human-comparable quality claims remain. However, v2 adds a central contribution that HopWeaver discovers diverse reasoning patterns exposing limitations of advanced RAG systems, and broadens its stated value to challenging benchmarks and targeted training in the abstract, introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 interprets RAG performance gaps as dependence on benchmark-specific reasoning patterns. Its error analysis acknowledges formatting effects and occasional insufficient evidence, qualifying v1's attribution to model errors. Limitations now discuss backbone/corpus dependence, inherited bias and English-only testing; the two-hop focus remains documented in Appendix B.

D1.justification: Appendix H adds concrete RAG settings, including Llama3-8B-Instruct, e5-base-v2, input length, retrieval depth and FlashRAG prompts. Appendix B newly explains benchmark question-type selection. Existing synthesis hyperparameters, hardware, cost information and code-access instructions are largely retained.

E1.justification: The English Wikipedia corpus, benchmark datasets and bridge/comparison coverage remain. Section 5.4 adds an end-to-end RAG scenario in which answers depend on retrieved context, extending the earlier separate retrieval and question-only/golden-document QA evaluations.

E2.justification: v2 Table 4 introduces a substantial new comparison involving Standard RAG, REPLUG, SuRe, FLARE and IRCoT. The comparator sets in the retained quality, retrieval and ablation experiments are unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include a separate 500-sample validation, 50 human-rated question pairs selected with LLM-score differences above 0.3, and a random 100-question reasoning-path audit. The RAG experiment introduces Llama3-8B-Instruct with a 2048-token input limit and top-five retrieval. Existing main evaluations are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds sample-size validation, human validation of the judge and manual reasoning-path assessment. It expands v1's brief GPT-4o error inspection into a quantified 49-case breakdown: 18 formatting differences, 29 reasoning errors and two insufficient-evidence cases. The original reranker and polisher ablations are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Table 9 extends reliability reporting to human evaluation through majority/unanimous agreement and three-rater Fleiss' kappa. The existing judge-stability procedure—five independent runs at temperature zero, with SD, alpha and kappa—is unchanged.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the retained ablation results are unchanged. New results include RAG scores, dataset statistics, 500-sample quality scores and human audits. For example, Table 4 reports bridge F1 of 0.318 for Standard RAG versus 0.158 for IRCoT; Table 10 reports 92% correct reasoning paths. Table 9 reports 94% human-majority agreement, although Section 4.1 inconsistently states 92%.

M1.justification: The synthesis steps, MMR retrieval, simulated-feedback reranker, filtering and polishing procedures remain unchanged. The clarified fallback between direct recommendation and diversified search was already specified in v1's prompt appendix.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution list, conclusion and limitations are rewritten. Related work becomes Section 2, preliminaries move to Appendix A, and main-text ablations move to Appendix C. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative while retaining most method and prompt descriptions.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the tabular presentation with RAG, dataset-statistics, larger-sample, human-agreement and reasoning-path tables. Existing ablation tables move to the appendix, and table captions and floats are repositioned. The core diagrams, radar plot and reliability heatmaps are retained.

R1.justification: A new three-part Related Works section substantially expands the previously scattered positioning around datasets, synthesis and evaluation. It distinguishes rule-based, neural, structured-resource and recent LLM approaches, adding works such as Du et al. (2017), Chen et al. (2024b) and HopRAG.

T1.justification: The comparison-path definition is corrected: v1 Equation 6 begins with the self-loop (e1, r1, e1), whereas v2 Appendix A Equation 8 uses (e1, r1, e2) and consistent terminal indices. The remaining constraints, retrieval equation, loss and reliability formulas are retained.

improvement.justification: The human judge-validation study and quantified reasoning-path audit address important gaps in v1's evidence for dataset quality. Larger-sample checks and end-to-end RAG tests further strengthen validation and practical relevance. These gains substantially improve the paper, although the 92%/94% agreement inconsistency and interpretation of RAG gaps as proof of reasoning-pattern diversity remain weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HopWeaver research. All 27 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support reliable comparison despite retitling and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds end-to-end RAG evaluation, larger-sample validation, human judgments and reasoning-path assessments.

before.justification: v1 reports original question-quality, QA, retrieval, reranker and polisher experiments, plus judge-reliability measurements in Appendix C.

results.title: HopWeaver: Cross-Document Synthesis of High-Quality and Authentic Multi-Hop Questions

C1.justification: v3's abstract, introduction, and conclusion elevate executable grounding's superiority to a central empirical contribution; v1 instead emphasizes general framework effectiveness and finds different prompts best for different extraction components. v3 also claims substantially broader regulatory coverage and emphasizes deployment without fine-tuning and recovery of long-range, non-linear dependencies.

C2.justification: v3 replaces much of the prompt interpretation with arguments about pseudo-code as a structural scaffold, equality over-merging, and abstraction-induced precision loss. It adds qualifications about P4 outperforming P5 in some dense cases. Limitations now explicitly cover quadratic pairwise scaling and omitted temporal constraints, exceptions, and probabilistic rules, while the earlier small-dataset limitation is removed.

D1.justification: v1 promises dataset release after acceptance; v3 states that both code and data are available and supplies a repository link, materially changing reported resource access. Appendices A.5–A.6 add text-quality criteria and annotation-processing explanations, and Figure 14 supplies the pseudo-code example's input. Conversely, v3 drops the explicit Macro-F1 specification. Resource availability is reported by the PDF and was not externally verified.

E1.justification: BPRF becomes BREX with substantially broader represented domains. Beyond v1's banking, healthcare, e-commerce, manufacturing, and service examples, v3 Section 3.2 explicitly includes scientific research management, administrative approvals, legal processes, and financial compliance across over 30 domains. The rule-extraction and dependency-identification tasks remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated model roster is largely replaced across all three tasks. v1's GPT-4o/o1, ERNIE, ChatGLM/GLM, Llama-3.1, Qwen2.5, QwQ, and DeepSeek-v3 comparisons give way to Gemini-2.5, GPT-5, Kimi-k2, DeepSeek-3.1/3.2-exp, and Qwen3 variants. DeepSeek-R1 remains. These changes appear in the actual result tables, not merely the references.

E3.justification: The evaluation corpus expands from 50 documents/326 rules to 409 documents/2,855 rules, and synthetic generation changes from ChatGPT-3.5 to Gemini-2.5-Pro. v3 adds rule-count and rule-pair-count stratification and evaluates the stricter atomic equality convention. Agreement assessment changes from annotating the dataset to an unspecified subset. v1 specifies Macro-F1 for classification; v3 says only F1, leaving any averaging change unresolved.

E4.justification: v3 adds dependency-type comparisons and systematic analyses of extraction performance versus rule density and dependency performance versus pair count (Figures 3–4). Appendix A.7 replaces v1's flight-booking, foreign-currency-deposit, and DeepSeek shopping analyses with leave, credit-card, and fixed-deposit cases examining equality over-merging and pseudo-code-induced spurious rules.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 4 introduces error bars and accompanying discussion of variability, whereas v1 provides point estimates and case scores without such dispersion displays. The bars' statistical meaning and calculation are unspecified. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, or significance tests; ICC and Fleiss' Kappa remain the annotation-agreement measures.

E6.justification: The experimental results are substantially replaced. v1 Tables 4–5 report P1 as best on average for NER (0.910) and P4 for logical classification (0.5947); v3 Tables 2–3 favor P5 (0.882 and 0.850). These are different corpora/model rosters, not same-setting performance changes. Dependency results, complexity findings, and case outcomes are also replaced or added. Reported ICC changes from 0.904 to 0.892 and Kappa from 0.911 to 0.901.

M1.justification: The two-stage extraction/dependency procedure and five prompting strategies remain. However, Prompt 4's demonstration changes from grouping b, c, and d into one equality rule in v1 Figure 11 to separate equality rules in v3 Figure 13, changing the extraction guidance. Pseudo-code prompting already existed in v1; its renaming as executable grounding is not a new component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around the Logic Gap and executable grounding. BPRF and prompt terminology are renamed, methodology and experiments gain dedicated subsections, and definitions move into an appendix expanded into A.1–A.7. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The dataset-construction and framework diagrams are redrawn, performance tables gain color shading, and the dependency table changes from a wide horizontal display to a vertical model list. New radar and complexity plots are added. Dataset statistics and annotation illustrations move to the appendix, case tables are replaced, and the earlier DeepSeek output/reasoning figures are removed. The three dependency-example diagrams are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: v3 adds a systematic comparison of eight existing benchmarks by size, modeling paradigm, and source (Appendix A.4, Table 6). It expands positioning against synthetic procedural datasets and schema-constrained instruction tuning, adding works including PET, ProcessTBench, and Pyrih et al. (2025). This goes beyond v1's narrative action-flow versus rule-flow distinction; the benchmark comparison is not an experimental baseline evaluation.

T1.justification: v3 explicitly normalizes complex conditions into atomic rules and specifies that equality operates on a single value (Appendices A.1 and A.7). This revises the semantics illustrated by grouped equality values in v1 Table 8 and Figure 11. The condition–action schema and dependency categories otherwise remain; added graph notation largely formalizes existing content, and no theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the limited empirical basis acknowledged in v1: broader regulatory coverage, matched Instruct/Thinking comparisons, systematic complexity tests, and concrete failure analyses make the findings more informative than aggregate scores and selected success cases alone. Clearer annotation guidance and reported code/data access also improve usefulness. Important weaknesses remain: error bars are undefined, and P5's small average leads in Tables 2–3 lack significance testing, limiting the stronger superiority claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ExIde business-rule extraction work. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, prompts, and appendices support comparison despite substantial benchmark and experimental revisions.

after.justification: v3 reports original evaluations of 13 LLMs in Tables 2–4, dependency-type and complexity analyses in Figures 3–4, annotation-quality measurements, and appendix case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 12 LLMs in Tables 4–6, annotation-quality measurements, and experimental case studies.

results.title: Business as Rulesual: A Benchmark and Framework for Business Rule Flow Modeling with LLMs

C1.justification: v2 adds a headline claim that ChainEval has the strongest correlation with expert judgments among tested metrics. Its abstract and conclusion emphasize finance- and math-tuned models substantially narrowing the frontier-model gap, revising v1's predominantly scale-driven account of general-purpose models outperforming specialized models. The central symbolic financial benchmark contribution remains.

C2.justification: v2 substantially revises explanations toward fine-tuning scope, domain accuracy versus generality, and structural alignment as a basis for metric validity. It adds specific limitations involving verbosity-inflated scores and repetitive outputs confusing regex parsing, with proposed parsing and length-penalty remedies. The earlier synthetic-data, numerical-task, and English/U.S. applicability limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the zero-shot prompt, regex step extraction, model identifiers and backbones (Table 3), expert qualifications, calibration and correction workflow, and human-rating rubrics (Appendices B–F). Project and leaderboard links supplement the retained code link. The template-generation prompt is retained, while the obsolete Claude verification prompt is removed. Newly disclosed prompting and parsing details alone do not establish changes to earlier runs.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from 54 to 58 topics by adding Stress Testing, Regulatory Compliance, Risk Appetite, and Risk Metrics within Risk Management (Figure 2). v2 also constrains questions to a single target value. The twelve domains and English, U.S.-based symbolic financial task remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated panel changes substantially from 30 to 26 models. v2 adds GPT-5 variants, Claude Sonnet models, Gemini 2.5, full DeepSeek models, Grok 4, and DianJin-R1, while removing Gemma variants, Mixtral, larger Llama models, o3/o4-mini, and FinanceConnect, among others. Its Finance-LlaMA and Finance-Qwen entries retain the WiroAI comparators under shorter names.

E3.justification: The primary scoring protocol changes to DTWNormGate, and ROUGE-Lsum disappears. v2 adds randomized, anonymized human assessment of 20 questions answered by five models and a separate 200-case comparison including Grok 4 Heavy. MetaMath's stated size changes from 13B to 7B, and fixed decoding settings gain an availability exception. Figure 4's ChainEval caption conflicts with its FAC axis, leaving that analysis's metric uncertain.

E4.justification: v2 adds human validation of ChainEval, gated-versus-soft and DTW-versus-non-DTW comparisons, template-error statistics, and analysis of verbosity and repetitive-step parsing failures (Section 5.2; Appendices D and G). The name-only, value-only, and combined perturbation experiment in v1 Section 5.3.4 and Table 2 is removed. Difficulty analysis remains with revised models and reporting.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly identifies Table 1 dispersions as standard deviations and introduces Spearman correlation estimation for human-rating and metric validation. Both versions retain ten random-seed instantiations per template; this does not establish additional repeated model runs. Neither provides confidence intervals or significance tests for the metric-ranking differences.

E6.justification: Benchmark results are extensively replaced under revised data and scoring. v2 Table 1 reports ChainEval scores of 58.65 for Gemini 2.5 Pro, 57.34 for Fin-R1, and 56.40 for Mathstral; these cannot be interpreted as gains over v1 FAC or Step-F1. New results include Grok 4 Heavy's 61.99 versus GPT-5's 60.60 on the shared 200-case subset and DTWNormGate's human correlation of 0.640. Earlier perturbation and comprehensive appendix domain results disappear.

M1.justification: Section 4 replaces independent maximum-similarity step matching and thresholded precision/recall/F1 with monotonic Dynamic Time Warping alignment and normalized gated path scoring. Section 3.3 also replaces Claude-triggered expert escalation with calibrated direct expert review and template corrections.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, construction narrative, and results discussion undergo extensive rewriting and compression. Model discussion is reorganized from six categories into four, metric validation precedes experimental setup, and the appendices are reorganized around expert auditing and metric evaluation. Author and affiliation text also changes.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned with fewer metric columns, a model-size column, and different groupings. The main radar display changes from two panels to one, the difficulty plot is redrawn, and the comprehensive appendix radar figures are removed. New displays cover model sources, annotation errors, metric correlations, and annotation interfaces. Figure 4 introduces a caption/axis mismatch between ChainEval and FAC.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds comparisons with TAT-QA, MultiHiertt, DocMath-Eval, and FinanceMath. References also change with the evaluated model panel. This broadens the discussion of adjacent benchmarks while retaining the central positioning around explicit, executable, domain-aware financial reasoning supervision.

T1.justification: The formal metric definition changes from independently maximized, thresholded step alignment to normalized minimum-cost DTW path alignment. Appendix G adds a weighted soft similarity definition with weights 0.85 and 0.15. Equation 4 also changes the relative-error denominator to the absolute gold value, correcting its behavior for negative values. These are substantive mathematical changes, although neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps: v1 lacks human validation of ChainEval and relies on Claude-flagged expert checking, whereas v2 reports comprehensive expert review with 29 template corrections and validation against 100 human-rated responses. The metric ablations, explicit rubrics, and model identifiers substantially strengthen empirical grounding and auditability. Removing perturbation and detailed domain results, and introducing Figure 4's metric-label inconsistency, weaken parts of the evaluation but do not outweigh these central gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FinChain and ChainEval. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained content across the substantial revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, a 200-case model comparison, expert template-audit outcomes, and human-rating correlations and metric ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 30 models on 2,700 generated cases, domain and difficulty analyses, and name/value perturbation experiments.

results.title: FinChain: A Symbolic Benchmark for Verifiable Chain-of-Thought Financial Reasoning

C1.justification: The introduction narrows its research-gap claim: v3 acknowledges temporally rich video diagnostics and complex reasoning benchmarks, emphasizing their lack of targeted user-feedback sycophancy evaluation. The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the benchmark and two mitigation contributions.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning systematic versus decoding-noise errors, response-format dependence, preservation of ordinary accuracy and regression in newer commercial models. It also introduces an orthogonality interpretation for steering and explicit limitations concerning white-box access, hour-scale videos and agentic tasks. These substantially extend the scientific discussion.

D1.justification: The abstract changes the supplied code-access location from GitHub to an anonymous.4open.science repository. v3 documents three-path voting and manual response classification for new experiments. Existing hardware, separate 100-video calibration set, selected layers and PCA settings remain documented.

E1.justification: The MSVD, MSRVTT and NExT-QA coverage, 367 videos, 6,367 questions and seven sycophancy scenarios are retained. Added experiments reuse this video-QA coverage; relaxed response formatting changes the protocol rather than the underlying task.

E2.justification: v3 Section 5.3/Table 4 adds majority voting and contradiction-checking prompting as evaluated alternatives to both mitigation methods on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Appendix G also adds Gemini-2.5-Flash to the commercial-model comparison. Existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: v3 adds neutral-question accuracy evaluation over 6,367 questions and a relaxed-response protocol with manual classification of misleading and non-committal answers across five scenarios. The new majority-vote comparator uses three sampled decoding paths. These expand evaluation procedures without replacing the original benchmark protocol.

results.title: VISTA: Verification In Sequential Turn-based Assessment

results.title: Cognitive Alpha Mining via LLM-Driven Code-Based Evolution

The original layer, direction, recency-bias, and explanation-length analyses are retained, often relocated.

Human scores, correlation coefficients, and some appendix Qwen statistics also change.

However, v1 specifies positive KV steering, while v3 specifies negative-KV suppression/subtraction but retains backbone-correct Q4 activations as positive and reports signed multipliers. These inconsistent conventions leave unclear whether the intervention changed or its description changed (Section 3.4; v3 Appendices C/O).

Methodological details and existing analyses are reorganized into expanded appendices, and separate analysis, limitations, ethics, acknowledgments, and author-contribution material changes the narrative structure substantially.

P2.justification: v3 changes the publication layout, redraws the framework diagram, adds motivating and baseline schematics, human-comparison charts, vector-similarity plots, and tables with computational-cost columns. Existing displays are also relocated: v1's layer and token visualizations reappear as v3 Figures 9 and 7.

It develops contrasts with ITI/CAA and discusses DeReC and JustiLM, while removing or reducing v1's traditional explainability, self-training/STaR, and DoLa/TruthfulQA positioning.

Most existing mathematical definitions remain, and no substantial theorem or proof development is introduced. The rewritten steering formalization also introduces the KV sign ambiguity noted under M1.

Steering documentation and explicit applicability limitations improve auditability. results.title: REFLEX: Self-Refining Explainable Fact-Checking via Verdict-Anchored Style Control

It also argues for protection through query rejection and limited effects of false activation. New Section 9 explicitly acknowledges untested extreme-scale knowledge bases and unassessed adversarial-editing and bias risks.

The retained UnKE batch size, temperature and gating threshold are unchanged, while the reported checkpoints omit T=1.

The loss ablation, layer study, cluster-threshold analysis, routing-scalability study and generated-answer cases are retained or relocated.

The intervention map, KL-regularized objective and clustering procedure remain unchanged. The relevance gate newly explained in the method section was already present in v1 Section 5.2.

P1.justification: Substantial paragraph rewriting spans the abstract, introduction, motivation, method, experiments and related work. Section 3 is reorganized around semantic locality and the geometric properties. v2 adds a limitations section and reorganizes appendix material into cost, configuration and routing subsections, moving the layer study out of the main text.

The main positioning around RLVR geometry and spectral PEFT remains. Author, year and publication changes for existing references do not represent new cited works.
